per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the CAP/DA clinical policy and checked amendments. The authoritative current document is Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, effective Sept. 1, 2025. I’m answering from the policy’s eligibility and coverage criteria sections.## General eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services

Under current NC Medicaid policy, a person generally must meet both the **waiver eligibility requirements** and the **specific Medicaid coverage criteria** for CAP/DA services. The controlling source is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), effective Sept. 1, 2025**, and I checked for amendments; the tool identifies this as the **current authoritative document**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### Core general eligibility requirements

A beneficiary must generally be:

- **Age 18 or older**
- **Enrolled in Medicaid Direct (fee-for-service Medicaid)**
- **In a CAP/DA target group** documented in the approved waiver
- **Eligible for Medicaid under the applicable Medicaid eligibility rules**
- **Determined to require an institutional level of care**, specifically the required **HCBS nursing facility level of care**
- **In need of long-term care supports** typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need
- **Reasonably expected to need at least one CAP/DA waiver service within 30 days** of the evaluation
- **Assigned a CAP/DA waiver slot**
- **Able to live safely in a private residence or approved location** with formal and informal supports
- **Exercising freedom of choice** to receive waiver services instead of institutional care. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### Service-plan and care-coordination requirements

The policy also requires that the person:

- Have a **signed service plan** authorizing **one or more waiver services** on a monthly basis, or in some cases short-term equipment/modification/technology to prevent institutional placement
- Have a service plan that helps **mitigate institutionalization through coordinated case management**
- Have a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services
- Have an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** for interruptions in care. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### Cost and safety requirements

The policy further says the person’s:

- **Paid care needs must be maintained within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver**
- **Health, safety, and well-being must be maintainable in the community setting** with the available supports. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## In short

A person is generally eligible for CAP/DA if they are an **adult Medicaid Direct beneficiary** who **meets Medicaid eligibility rules**, **needs nursing-facility level care**, **can safely remain at home or another approved community setting with supports**, **needs waiver services**, **has an approved service plan**, and **has a waiver slot**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

If you want, I can also break this down into:
1. **financial/Medicaid eligibility vs. functional eligibility**, or  
2. **what documents or assessments are usually used to prove CAP/DA eligibility**.

## Specifically not covered
Per **Section 4.2.1**:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** kept available at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as described in the policy’s care-coordination section

## General criteria that must be met for coverage
Under **Section 3.2.1**, orthotic/prosthetic items are covered only if they meet these baseline requirements:

- They are **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- They are **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s **medical, physical, or functional level**
- They are **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- There has been a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary and the ordering physician/PA/NP **within 6 months before** starting orthotics/prosthetics
- The beneficiary’s need for the item is **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician/PA/NP

- **Orthotic devices** must be needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** must replace all or part of the function of a **permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must need the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**
- The device must be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the treatment plan
  - **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms
  - of **high quality**, with **replacement parts available and obtainable**
- For reimbursement, the provider must be **enrolled as an appropriate board-certified provider** for the specific device

Cited source: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.

## Broader general noncoverage rules
The policy also says coverage is denied if, generally:

- the beneficiary does **not** meet eligibility requirements in Section 2.0
- the beneficiary does **not** meet the criteria in Section 3.0
- the item/service **duplicates another provider’s** item or service
- the item/service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

Cited source: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.1.

## Bottom line
So, under the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy, NC Medicaid does **not** cover comfort/convenience items, backup or duplicate devices, nursing-facility resident devices/supplies, items paid by another agency, or hospice-related equipment/supplies under this policy. - The beneficiary is making **satisfactory progress** toward goals and the documentation supports continuing treatment.

### 2) Prior approval still applies under EPSDT

> “If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.”

Policy 10A section **3.1.2 (“Ordering Practitioners”)** lists the practitioners who may order outpatient specialized therapies:

- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**

- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the congregate-settings PCS policy and confirmed the current authoritative documents by checking amendments on both PCS policies. Next I’ll answer using the congregate-settings eligibility section, plus the general PCS non-covered-services section to clarify limits like room and board.## Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for someone living in an assisted living-type setting, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS rules.

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate PCS policy, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who resides in certain **licensed congregate facilities**, including an **Adult Care Home (ACH)** or **combination home**, and in some licensed group homes, if the person also meets the medical/functional eligibility criteria. See **Section 3.2.1, “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid,”** in [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

### What that means in practice
A beneficiary in an assisted living facility is **not automatically covered** just because they live there. The policy says the person must, among other things:

- have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing unmet needs;
- need help with enough qualifying **activities of daily living (ADLs)**;
- live in a qualifying **licensed congregate facility**;
- have needs directly linked to the documented condition;
- be under a physician’s ongoing care;
- be medically stable; and
- not have another payer responsible for PCS.  
Source: **3L-1, Section 3.2.1** in [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

### Referral/assessment requirement
The congregate PCS policy also requires a referral and assessment process. A physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant referral is required, and once referred, the PCS assessment must be performed in the beneficiary’s congregate facility. See **Section 5.4.2, “Requirement for Physician Referral,”** in [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

### Important limit
Even when PCS is covered, **room and board are not covered** as PCS. See **Section 4.2.2, “Services not covered by Medicaid,”** in [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3l-state-plan-personal-care-services-pcs/download?attachment) (effective Jan. 1, 2026).

## Bottom line
**Yes, NC Medicaid may cover PCS for a beneficiary living in an assisted living facility,** if the facility is a qualifying licensed congregate setting and the beneficiary meets the PCS medical/functional criteria and referral/assessment requirements. But **Medicaid PCS does not cover room and board.**

- **A copy of the treatment plan**
- **A copy of the order for OST services**

- The **signature and credentials** of the person providing each service  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 7.2, effective Feb. 1, 2025)

Under **Policy 10A**, the plan of care must be a written, signed treatment plan covering a period of **no more than six months** and must spell out the diagnosis, goals, interventions, frequency, visit length, and the treating professional’s credentials/signature.   - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and

Next I’m going to read that section in full and check amendments for the regulation document so I can cite it as current.Under federal Medicaid regulations, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 CFR 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary:

1. **At the beneficiary’s place of residence**, as defined in **42 CFR 440.70(c)**; and  
2. **Pursuant to appropriate written orders and a written plan of care**, depending on the type of service. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

Those home health services include:

- **Part-time or intermittent nursing services**
- **Home health aide services**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances**
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services** (this category is optional for states)  
  [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Where must they be provided?

Federal law says they must be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** But that term is defined broadly.

### Not included as a place of residence
A beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**
- a **nursing facility**
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**

There is a limited exception for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

### Included / broader rule
The regulation also says nothing should be read to prohibit home health services **“in any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid inpatient payment includes room and board**.  

It further states that **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Bottom line
Federal Medicaid law defines home health services in **42 CFR 440.70** as specified nursing, aide, supplies/equipment, and certain therapy services provided under appropriate orders and a plan of care, and furnished at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**. That can include **any setting where normal life activities occur**, not just the person’s private home, but **not** hospitals, nursing facilities, ICF/IIDs (subject to a narrow exception), or other inpatient settings with room-and-board payment. For NC Medicaid hospice eligibility, the operative standard is that the person has a **prognosis of a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the terminal illness runs its normal course**. That wording appears in the federal hospice certification rule that NC Medicaid hospice policy tracks. [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418), § 418.22(b)(1).

NC Medicaid’s current hospice clinical policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Hospice Services**, effective **March 15, 2024**, and I checked the corpus for amendments to that policy and found **no listed amendments**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment).

## What certification is required

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **2 calendar days after a period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those 2 days, and the **written certification** must still be obtained before the claim is submitted. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1; [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418), § 418.22(a).

### Who must certify
For the **initial 90-day period**, NC Medicaid requires written certification from:
- **the hospice medical director or the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- **the individual’s attending physician, if the individual has one**.

For **subsequent periods**, only certification by:
- **the hospice medical director**, or
- **the physician member of the hospice IDG**
is required. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

### What the certification must contain
The certification/recertification must include:
- a **physician narrative** briefly synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s attestation that the narrative was composed after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- content reflecting the **beneficiary’s individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the **signature and date** of the certifying or recertifying physician. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), Attachment B, “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

The federal regulation also requires supporting clinical documentation and states the certification must specify a prognosis of **6 months or less** if the illness runs its normal course. [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418), § 418.22(b)(1)-(3).

### Timing rules
- Initial certifications: no more than **15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications: no more than **15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1 and Attachment B; [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418), § 418.22(a)(3).

### Face-to-face requirement
For the **3rd benefit period recertification and every recertification after that**, a **hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner** must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary **before, but no more than 30 calendar days before**, the recertification, to gather clinical findings supporting continued eligibility. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1; [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418), § 418.22(a)(4).

## Bottom line
NC Medicaid hospice eligibility uses the standard that the beneficiary is **expected to live 6 months or less if the illness follows its normal course**, and hospice must obtain the required **physician certification of terminal illness** for each benefit period, with specific rules about **who signs**, **what must be included**, and **when it must be completed**.
